claim: In adult Drosophila females, the midgut is dramatically remodelled to enhance reproductive output.
source: In this study, we show that, in adult Drosophila females, the midgut is dramatically remodelled to enhance reproductive output.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript including proliferation assays, size measurements, and fecundity experiments.

claim: Organ remodelling does not occur in response to increased nutrient intake and/or offspring demands, but rather precedes them.
source: In contrast to extant models, organ remodelling does not occur in response to increased nutrient intake and/or offspring demands, but rather precedes them.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in sterile ovoD1 mutant flies showing that intestinal remodelling occurs even in the absence of egg production and increased food intake.

claim: Juvenile hormone (JH) is an anticipatory endocrine signal released after mating.
source: With spatially and temporally directed manipulations, we identify juvenile hormone (JH) as an anticipatory endocrine signal released after mating.
evidence: This is supported by DART mass spectrometry data showing increased circulating JH levels in mated females compared to virgins.

claim: JH signals directly to intestinal progenitors through bHLH-PAS domain proteins Methoprene-tolerant (Met) and Germ cell-expressed (Gce) to yield a larger organ.
source: Acting through intestinal bHLH-PAS domain proteins Methoprene-tolerant (Met) and Germ cell-expressed (Gce), JH signals directly to intestinal progenitors to yield a larger organ
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific RNAi experiments showing that downregulation of Met or Gce in intestinal progenitors prevents mating-induced proliferation and gut size increase.

claim: JH adjusts gene expression and sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) activity in enterocytes to support increased lipid metabolism.
source: and adjusts gene expression and sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) activity in enterocytes to support increased lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assays showing increased SREBP activity and qPCR data showing upregulation of lipid metabolism genes after mating.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster females can lay up to 100 eggs per day at the peak of their fertility in early life.
source: Drosophila melanogaster females can lay up to 100 eggs per day at the peak of their fertility in early life (David et al., 1974; Klepsatel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mating increases the number of both dividing and differentiating midgut cells.
source: We found that mating increases the number of both dividing and differentiating midgut cells, as revealed by phospho-Histone H3 (pH3) stainings and temporal analyses of progenitors and their descendants using the dual-labelling system escargot-Repressible Dual Differential Marker (esgReDDM, Antonello et al., 2015) (Figure 1A,C,E).
evidence: This is supported by pH3 staining data and esgReDDM tracing experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The midgut of mated females becomes visibly larger.
source: The midgut of mated females also becomes visibly larger; gut diameter measurements were suggestive of a net increase in the number of postmitotic intestinal cells (Figure 1B,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by gut diameter measurements and cell counts shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mating triggers activation of SREBP in the midgut.
source: Concurrent with midgut re-sizing, we observed mating-dependent activation of the single Drosophila homologue of the mammalian family of sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs [Theopold et al., 1996; Shimano, 2001; Seegmiller et al., 2002], also known as HLH106 in flies, Figure 2A,B), using a reporter subject to the same physiologically regulated proteolytic processing as wild-type SREBP (Kunte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by SREBP reporter expression data shown in Figure 2A,B and citations to previous work characterizing SREBP.

claim: SREBP activation after mating is accompanied by upregulation of midgut transcripts involved in fatty acid synthesis and activation.
source: SREBP activation after mating was accompanied by upregulation of midgut transcripts involved in fatty acid synthesis and activation (SREBP, the long-chain fatty acid CoA ligases bubblegum (bgm) and Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain (Acsl) and, depending on genetic background, Fatty acid synthase (FAS) and Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)) (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Many upregulated lipid metabolism genes are known SREBP targets in flies and/or mammals.
source: many of which are known SREBP targets in flies and/or mammals (Seegmiller et al., 2002; Horton et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Enterocytes located in the posterior midgut region (R5) are preferential sites of transcriptional and SREBP activity changes.
source: Immunohistochemical analyses using reporters pointed to the ECs located in the posterior midgut region (R5, Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013) as preferential sites of transcriptional and SREBP activity changes (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression patterns shown in Figure 2A-D and citations to previous work defining midgut regions.

claim: Changes in intestinal progenitors and their progeny in female flies parallel those observed in mammals leading to hyperplasia.
source: Thus, in female flies actively engaged in reproduction, changes in both intestinal progenitors and their progeny parallel those observed in mammals leading to hyperplasia (Hammond, 1997; Speakman, 2008)
evidence: This claim draws a comparison to mammalian systems based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in intestinal progenitors and their progeny in female flies parallel those observed in mammals leading to increased organ size.
source: Thus, in female flies actively engaged in reproduction, changes in both intestinal progenitors and their progeny parallel those observed in mammals leading to hyperplasia (Hammond, 1997; Speakman, 2008), increased organ size (Hammond, 1997; Speakman, 2008)
evidence: This claim draws a comparison to mammalian systems based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in intestinal progenitors and their progeny in female flies parallel those observed in mammals leading to upregulation of lipid gene expression.
source: and upregulation of lipid gene expression (Athippozhy et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim draws a comparison to mammalian systems based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: The synthesis of juvenile hormone (JH) in the corpus allatum can be stimulated ex vivo by the male-derived Sex Peptide.
source: The synthesis of juvenile hormone (JH) in the corpus allatum, an endocrine gland, can be stimulated ex vivo by the male-derived Sex Peptide, suggesting regulation by mating (Moshitzky et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The levels of in vivo circulating JH are increased after mating.
source: Using rapid direct analysis in real time (DART) mass spectrometry, we profiled haemolymph of both virgin and mated female flies and established that the levels of in vivo circulating JH are indeed increased after mating (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by DART mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transcript upregulation of the JH target Kruppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1) occurs in guts of mated females.
source: Consistent with a possible intestinal role, we detected transcript upregulation of the JH target Kruppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1) (Jindra et al., 2013) in guts of mated females (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation identifying Kr-h1 as a JH target.

claim: Feeding methoprene (a JH analogue) to virgin female flies leads to effects on intestinal progenitors, gut diameter, and lipid metabolism comparable to those triggered by mating.
source: To explore the roles of JH signalling on intestinal remodelling, we first fed methoprene, a JH analogue (JHa) (Cerf and Georghiou, 1972), to virgin female flies. This led to effects on intestinal progenitors, gut diameter, and lipid metabolism comparable to those triggered by mating (Figure 3B–E,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-E,H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and a citation identifying methoprene as a JH analogue.

claim: Genetic ablation of the corpus allatum results in adult-specific reduction of JH titres in the haemolymph.
source: We next blocked endogenous JH production by mis-expressing the protein phosphatase inhibitor NiPp1 using the corpus allatum-specific driver Aug21-Gal4 (Siegmund and Korge, 2001): a genetic manipulation known to result in adult-specific ablation of the corpus allatum and a dramatic reduction of JH titres in the haemolymph (Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies characterizing the genetic manipulation.

claim: Depletion of systemic JH prevents mating-triggered remodelling.
source: Depletion of systemic JH prevented mating-triggered remodelling: a phenotype that could be restored in these gland-ablated flies by JHa feeding (Figure 3F,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,I.

claim: The phenotype of mating-triggered remodelling can be restored in gland-ablated flies by JHa feeding.
source: Depletion of systemic JH prevented mating-triggered remodelling: a phenotype that could be restored in these gland-ablated flies by JHa feeding (Figure 3F,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,I.

claim: Downregulation of Met or gce in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation.
source: Downregulation of either gce or Met in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation (G, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments and proliferation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Downregulation of Met or gce in adult progenitors abrogates gut size increase.
source: and gut size increase (J, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments and gut size measurements shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is abolished by the downregulation of gce, but not Met, in ECs.
source: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is abolished by the downregulation of gce, but not Met, in ECs using the EC-specific driver Mex-Gal4 (K–K′′′′).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Intestinal progenitors with downregulated JH receptors remain competent to respond to homeostatic machinery that maintains gut integrity.
source: Intestinal progenitors with downregulated JH receptors were found in numbers comparable to those of controls in virgin females and were able to increase their proliferation in response to a JH-unrelated stimulus: the ROS-inducing compound paraquat (Biteau et al., 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This indicates that they remain competent to respond to the well-studied homeostatic machinery that maintains gut integrity (Jiang and Edgar, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by paraquat damage experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Mating- and damage-induced proliferative mechanisms may differ and can be uncoupled.
source: and suggests that mating- and damage-induced proliferative mechanisms may differ and can be uncoupled.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that progenitors with downregulated JH receptors can respond to paraquat but not mating.

claim: The mating-triggered changes in proliferation, midgut size, and SREBP activity are all still apparent in sterile female ovoD1 mutant flies.
source: Consistent with the latter idea, the mating-triggered changes in proliferation, midgut size, and SREBP activity are all still apparent in sterile female ovoD1 mutant flies in which egg production is blocked prior to vitellogenesis and which do not increase food intake after mating (Barnes et al., 2008) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experiments in ovoD1 mutants shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation to previous work characterizing these mutants.

claim: EC-specific downregulation of JH receptors or SREBP leads to a reduction in the number (but not viability) of eggs produced.
source: To investigate the significance of intestinal remodelling, we used several RNAi transgenes to downregulate either the JH receptors or SREBP, which is activated by mating, specifically in adult ECs. In all cases, EC-specific downregulation led to a reduction in the number (but not viability) of eggs produced (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by fecundity and egg viability experiments shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: JH signalling is required to specifically enhance the quantity (fecundity), but not the quality (viability), of reproductive output.
source: indicating that JH signalling is required to specifically enhance the quantity (fecundity), but not the quality (viability), of reproductive output.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EC-specific downregulation of JH receptors reduces egg number but not viability.

claim: Sterile ovoD1 female flies accumulate peripheral fat after mating.
source: Consistent with this idea, sterile ovoD1 female flies accumulate peripheral fat after mating (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is supported by thin-layer chromatography data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Lipid accumulation in the posterior midgut can be induced in sterile flies by treatment with JHa.
source: and lipid accumulation in the posterior midgut could be induced in fertile flies by either treatment of these sterile flies with JHa or by knocking down lipid shuttling proteins acutely, thereby blocking all lipid circulation (Palm et al., 2012) (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4G-J and a citation to previous work on lipid shuttling.

claim: Lipid accumulation in the posterior midgut can be induced by knocking down lipid shuttling proteins acutely.
source: and lipid accumulation in the posterior midgut could be induced in fertile flies by either treatment of these sterile flies with JHa or by knocking down lipid shuttling proteins acutely, thereby blocking all lipid circulation (Palm et al., 2012) (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4G-J and a citation to previous work on lipid shuttling.

claim: The metabolic reprogramming of ECs by JH supports fecundity.
source: Together, these data show that the metabolic reprogramming of ECs by JH supports fecundity, thus confirming that intestinal plasticity is required to sustain reproductive output at the time of peak fertility.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of JH receptor and SREBP knockdown experiments showing reduced fecundity.

claim: Intestinal plasticity is required to sustain reproductive output at the time of peak fertility.
source: Together, these data show that the metabolic reprogramming of ECs by JH supports fecundity, thus confirming that intestinal plasticity is required to sustain reproductive output at the time of peak fertility.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing that blocking intestinal remodelling reduces fecundity.

claim: The importance of intestinal lipogenesis is becoming increasingly recognised in both flies and mammals.
source: The importance of intestinal lipogenesis is becoming increasingly recognised in both flies and mammals (Lodhi et al., 2011; Palm et al., 2012; Sieber and Thummel, 2012; Song et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intestinal lipogenesis underpins reproductive output.
source: and here we show that it underpins reproductive output.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that blocking lipid metabolism in the intestine reduces fecundity.

claim: Upregulation of SREBP target genes has been reported in the small intestine of lactating rats.
source: Notably, upregulation of SREBP target genes has been reported in the small intestine of lactating rats (Athippozhy et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The findings on intestinal remodelling during reproduction may be conserved beyond insects.
source: suggesting that our findings may be conserved beyond insects.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity to observations in lactating rats.

claim: Mating enhances egg production tenfold in Drosophila.
source: Drosophila may experience a particularly extreme example of this shift after mating: an event that enhances egg production tenfold and triggers multiple metabolic and behavioural adaptations (Kubli, 2003; Rogina et al., 2007; Avila et al., 2011; Cognigni et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mating triggers multiple metabolic and behavioural adaptations in Drosophila.
source: Drosophila may experience a particularly extreme example of this shift after mating: an event that enhances egg production tenfold and triggers multiple metabolic and behavioural adaptations (Kubli, 2003; Rogina et al., 2007; Avila et al., 2011; Cognigni et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Post-mating changes are in large part brought about by signals delivered by the male during copulation, in particular the Sex Peptide.
source: These changes are in large part brought about by signals delivered by the male during copulation, in particular the Sex Peptide (Kubli, 2003; Avila et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several reports connect SP to the corpus allatum and JH production.
source: Several reports connect SP to the corpus allatum and JH production (Moshitzky et al., 1996; Bontonou et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The systemic effects of mating via SP could be carried out through the JH pathway.
source: suggesting that the systemic effects of mating via SP could be carried out through this pathway.
evidence: This is speculated based on the connection between SP and JH production.

claim: JH knockdown in females extends female lifespan while reducing reproductive output and/or peak fertility.
source: Intriguingly, both JH knockdown in females (Yamamoto et al., 2013) and SP deficiency in males (Wigby and Chapman, 2005) extend female lifespan while reducing reproductive output and/or peak fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SP deficiency in males extends female lifespan while reducing reproductive output and/or peak fertility.
source: Intriguingly, both JH knockdown in females (Yamamoto et al., 2013) and SP deficiency in males (Wigby and Chapman, 2005) extend female lifespan while reducing reproductive output and/or peak fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The 'cost of mating' on lifespan is not relieved by sterility.
source: This 'cost of mating' on lifespan is not relieved by sterility (Ueyama and Fuyama, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Physiological effects in non-reproductive tissues are responsible for the cost of mating on lifespan.
source: suggesting that physiological effects in non-reproductive tissues are responsible.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sterility does not relieve the cost of mating on lifespan.

claim: The intestinal reprogramming represents a novel physiological target of postmating plasticity ideally placed at the interface between nutrition and reproduction.
source: The intestinal reprogramming that we describe here represents a novel physiological target of postmating plasticity ideally placed at the interface between nutrition and reproduction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: Ageing in flies is accompanied by reduced fertility.
source: Ageing in flies is accompanied by reduced fertility (Economos et al., 1979) and intestinal dysplasia (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ageing in flies is accompanied by intestinal dysplasia.
source: Ageing in flies is accompanied by reduced fertility (Economos et al., 1979) and intestinal dysplasia (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic manipulations that affect intestinal progenitors can affect lifespan.
source: and genetic manipulations that affect intestinal progenitors can affect lifespan (Biteau et al., 2010; Rera et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In larvae, the corpora allata integrate age and metabolic status information to optimise developmental progression.
source: In larvae, the corpora allata integrate age and metabolic status information to optimise developmental progression (Mirth and Shingleton, 2012; Sarraf-Zadeh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In adults, the corpus allatum acts as a nexus that detects changes in the organism's circumstances and condition to alter its metabolic and/or reproductive set points.
source: Increasing evidence is revealing that, in adults, this insect endocrine organ acts as a nexus that detects changes in the organism's circumstances and condition to alter its metabolic and/or reproductive set points.
evidence: This is a general statement based on accumulating evidence in the field.

claim: The corpus allatum alters metabolic and reproductive set points through regulated release of JH.
source: It does so through regulated release of JH, with pleiotropic effects on ovarian maturation, adipose tissue, learning and memory, diapause, innate immunity, and ageing (Nijhout and Riddiford, 1974; Jowett and Postlethwait, 1980; Fahrbach and Robinson, 1996; Wyatt and Davey, 1996; Flatt et al., 2005; Riddiford, 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some effects of JH may be modulated by crosstalk between JH and other systemic signals such as insulin-like peptides and ecdysteroids.
source: Some of these effects may be modulated by crosstalk between JH and other systemic signals such as insulin-like peptides and ecdysteroids (Jindra et al., 2013; Koyama et al., 2013; Mirth et al., 2014; Rauschenbach et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cellular and molecular targets of JH action remain incompletely understood.
source: but the cellular and molecular targets of JH action remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Insect JH has been compared to mammalian thyroid hormones based on structural and functional similarities.
source: Based on structural and functional similarities, insect JH has been compared to mammalian thyroid hormones (Flatt et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Thyroid hormones are key energy balance regulators often associated with gastrointestinal alterations when pathologically dysregulated.
source: key energy balance regulators often associated with gastrointestinal alterations when pathologically dysregulated (Middleton, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in thyroid function occur during human pregnancy.
source: Given the well-established changes in thyroid function during human pregnancy (Glinoer, 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Relay of JH signalling in the intestine may differ from the classical model in which Met and gce act redundantly.
source: Downstream of its receptor(s), relay of JH signalling in the intestine may differ from the classical model in which Met and gce act redundantly (Abdou et al., 2011; Jindra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that downregulation of either Met or gce alone is sufficient to prevent mating-induced changes, and is contrasted with citations to previous work describing redundancy.

claim: Downregulation of either Met or gce alone is sufficient to prevent the mating-induced changes in intestinal progenitors.
source: Indeed, downregulation of either gene alone is sufficient to prevent the mating-induced changes in intestinal progenitors: a finding that we confirmed by observing that viable Met27 mutants also fail to undergo mating-induced remodelling (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments and mutant analysis.

claim: Viable Met27 mutants fail to undergo mating-induced remodelling.
source: a finding that we confirmed by observing that viable Met27 mutants also fail to undergo mating-induced remodelling (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claim: The actions of Met and Gce may be cell-specific.
source: The actions of Met and Gce may also be cell-specific, as suggested by a preferential requirement for gce in ECs
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gce, but not Met, is required for bgm reporter upregulation in ECs.

claim: Cell-specific actions of Met and Gce may result from different Met/gce expression levels and/or interacting partners.
source: and may result from different Met/gce expression levels (our unpublished observations) and/or interacting partners.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Taiman is homologous to the mammalian steroid receptor coactivator 1 (SRC-1)/NCoA-1/p160.
source: Candidates to consider include Taiman, homologous to the mammalian steroid receptor coactivator 1 (SRC-1)/NCoA-1/p160 (Charles et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circadian clock proteins are Met-binding partners that coordinate the switch from diapause to reproduction in other insects.
source: and, more intriguingly, circadian clock proteins: Met-binding partners recently shown to coordinate the switch from diapause to reproduction in other insects (Shin et al., 2012; Bajgar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Examples of changes in intestinal size and nutrient utilisation are widespread across the animal kingdom in response to both environmental and internal challenges.
source: Adult organ plasticity is not a peculiarity of Drosophila reproduction; examples of changes in intestinal size and nutrient utilisation are widespread across the animal kingdom in response to both environmental and internal challenges (Carey, 1990; Hammond, 1997; Piersma and Lindstrom, 1997; Speakman, 2008; O'Brien et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in gut microbiota are observed during human pregnancy.
source: Although intestinal remodelling has not been assessed in human pregnancy, it could be one of the major drivers for the changes in gut microbiota observed during pregnancy (Koren et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study, and the connection to intestinal remodelling is speculated.

claim: Intestinal remodelling could be one of the major drivers for changes in gut microbiota during pregnancy.
source: Although intestinal remodelling has not been assessed in human pregnancy, it could be one of the major drivers for the changes in gut microbiota observed during pregnancy (Koren et al., 2012)
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Changes in gastrointestinal physiology are common during pregnancy.
source: and could contribute to changes in gastrointestinal physiology, common during pregnancy (Keller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Resetting of anatomical or metabolic features of internal organs may be a broadly used strategy to achieve a positive energy balance.
source: Resetting of anatomical or metabolic features of internal organs may thus be a broadly used strategy to achieve a positive energy balance which, when matched to the developing offspring's demands, will contribute to reproductive success.
evidence: This is a general interpretation of the findings.

claim: Weight gain and increased fat mass have been observed upon gonadectomy of multiple species including mice, rats, cats, monkeys, and other mammals.
source: However, if deployed in the absence of such demands, organ remodelling could contribute to the weight gain and increased fat mass that has been observed upon gonadectomy of multiple species including mice, rats, cats, monkeys, and other mammals (Hansen et al., 2013 and references therein).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Organ remodelling could contribute to weight gain and increased fat mass upon gonadectomy.
source: However, if deployed in the absence of such demands, organ remodelling could contribute to the weight gain and increased fat mass that has been observed upon gonadectomy of multiple species including mice, rats, cats, monkeys, and other mammals (Hansen et al., 2013 and references therein).
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: Inappropriate persistence of metabolic remodelling beyond pregnancy and lactation could contribute to post-pregnancy weight retention in humans.
source: In a more physiological context, inappropriate persistence of such metabolic remodelling beyond pregnancy and lactation could similarly contribute to post-pregnancy weight retention in humans—a phenotype that, at least in mice, is correlated with enhanced intestinal function (Casirola and Ferraris, 2003; Gore et al., 2003).
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism, with citations to previous studies showing correlation in mice.

claim: Post-pregnancy weight retention in mice is correlated with enhanced intestinal function.
source: a phenotype that, at least in mice, is correlated with enhanced intestinal function (Casirola and Ferraris, 2003; Gore et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inappropriate persistence of JH-like mechanisms that change the homeostatic set point of adult stem cells and their progeny to transform an organ may help explain why pregnancy changes the susceptibility to certain cancers.
source: Similarly, inappropriate persistence of JH-like mechanisms that change the homeostatic set point of adult stem cells and their progeny to transform an organ may also help explain why pregnancy changes the susceptibility to certain cancers (Gwinn et al., 1990).
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism, with a citation to a previous study on pregnancy and cancer susceptibility.

claim: Pregnancy changes the susceptibility to certain cancers.
source: may also help explain why pregnancy changes the susceptibility to certain cancers (Gwinn et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: At 3 days after mating, the posterior midgut of mated flies contains more newly generated postmitotic progeny compared to age-matched virgins.
source: At 3 days after mating, the posterior midgut of mated flies contains more newly generated postmitotic progeny (A) compared to age-matched virgins (A′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A,A' using the esgReDDM tracer system.

claim: At 3 days after mating, the midgut has become visibly larger.
source: It has also become visibly larger (B, B′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B,B'.

claim: At 3 days after mating, guts have a higher number of nuclei marked by the mitotic marker pH3 in both w1118 and OregonR backgrounds.
source: At this time point, these guts also have a higher number of nuclei marked by the mitotic marker pH3 in both w1118 and OregonR backgrounds (C, p = 0.008, and E, p < 0.001, negative binomial GLM)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C,E with statistical analysis.

claim: The proliferation increase after mating is transient.
source: although the proliferation increase is transient (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data.

claim: The size increase is quantified in the posterior midgut by measuring midgut diameter.
source: The size increase is quantified in the posterior midgut by measuring midgut diameter (D, p < 0.001, t-test)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: The size increase is quantified by counting the number of cells labelled by the EC marker caudal-Gal4.
source: and counting the number of cells labelled by the EC marker caudal-Gal4 (F, p = 0.02, t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in gut size at 3 days after mating is measurable and significant in the OregonR background.
source: The increase in gut size at 3 days after mating is also measurable (A, A′) and significant (B, p < 0.001, t-test) in the OregonR background.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: Mated guts contain more cells generated in the last 7 days if the fly had been mated in that time than if it had not.
source: The esgReDDM tracing system reveals that mated guts contain more cells generated in the last 7 days if the fly had been mated in that time (C, p < 0.001, t-test) than if it had not.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: The size increase is not due to stretching of the tissue, as the density of nuclei in the posterior midgut remains the same.
source: The size increase is not due to stretching of the tissue, as the density of nuclei in the posterior midgut remains the same (D, p = 0.77, t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: At 3 days after mating, increased expression of a SREBP reporter is apparent in the posterior midgut.
source: At 3 days after mating, increased expression of a reporter that replicates the transcriptional regulation and post-translational modification of sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) is apparent in the posterior midgut (A, A′, quantified in B, p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A,A',B with statistical analysis.

claim: A bgm transcriptional reporter is increased specifically in the ECs of the posterior midgut following mating.
source: A bgm transcriptional reporter is also increased specifically in the ECs of the posterior midgut following mating (C, C′, quantified in D, p = 0.002, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,C',D with statistical analysis.

claim: Transcript abundance of SREBP, bgm, and Acsl is increased by mating in the w1118 background.
source: Transcript abundance of SREBP, bgm, and the SREBP targets Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain (Acsl), Fatty acid synthase (FAS), and Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is increased by mating in either one or both of the w1118 and OregonR backgrounds (E w1118: p = 0.02 SREBP, p = 0.02 bgm, p = 0.005 Acsl, p = 0.5 FAS, p = 0.3 ACC
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with qPCR data and statistical analysis.

claim: Transcript abundance of SREBP, bgm, Acsl, FAS, and ACC is increased by mating in the OregonR background.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F with qPCR data and statistical analysis.

claim: Circulating juvenile hormone (JH) is elevated after mating in the haemolymph of female flies.
source: Circulating juvenile hormone (JH) is elevated after mating in the haemolymph of female flies (A, p = 0.02 at 24 hr, p = 0.002 at 48 hr, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with DART mass spectrometry data and statistical analysis.

claim: Increased tissue renewal is apparent following a 3-day dietary supplementation with JH analogue (JHa).
source: Increased tissue renewal (B, B′) and SREBP activation (C, C′, quantified in D, p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney test) are apparent following a 3-day dietary supplementation with JH analogue (JHa).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B,B' with esgReDDM tracing data.

claim: SREBP activation is apparent following a 3-day dietary supplementation with JHa.
source: Increased tissue renewal (B, B′) and SREBP activation (C, C′, quantified in D, p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney test) are apparent following a 3-day dietary supplementation with JH analogue (JHa).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C,C',D with reporter data and statistical analysis.

claim: JHa treatment is sufficient to increase mitoses in the posterior midgut.
source: JHa treatment is sufficient to increase mitoses (E, p < 0.001, negative binomial GLM) and size (H, p < 0.001, t-test) of the posterior midgut.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E with pH3 staining data and statistical analysis.

claim: JHa treatment is sufficient to increase size of the posterior midgut.
source: JHa treatment is sufficient to increase mitoses (E, p < 0.001, negative binomial GLM) and size (H, p < 0.001, t-test) of the posterior midgut.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H with gut diameter measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: When the endogenous JH source is genetically ablated, the proliferation increase that follows mating is abolished.
source: Conversely, when the endogenous JH source is genetically ablated by means of Aug21 > NiPp1 (Yamamoto et al., 2013), the proliferation and size increase that follow mating are abolished, although they can be reinstated by feeding JHa (proliferation F, p < 0.001 between Aug21/+ and Aug21 > NiPp1 mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and NiPp1/+ mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and Aug21 > NiPp1 + JHa mated; all relevant comparisons between virgins are not significant, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with pH3 staining data and statistical analysis, with citation to previous work on the genetic manipulation.

claim: When the endogenous JH source is genetically ablated, the size increase that follows mating is abolished.
source: gut diameter I, p = 0.002 between Aug21/+ and Aug21 > NiPp1 mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and NiPp1/+ mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and Aug21 > NiPp1 + JHa mated; all relevant comparisons between virgins are not significant, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3I with gut diameter measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The proliferation and size increase can be reinstated by feeding JHa to gland-ablated flies.
source: although they can be reinstated by feeding JHa (proliferation F, p < 0.001 between Aug21/+ and Aug21 > NiPp1 mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and NiPp1/+ mated, p < 0.001 between Aug21 > NiPp1 and Aug21 > NiPp1 + JHa mated
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F,I with experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Downregulation of gce in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation.
source: Downregulation of either gce or Met in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation (G, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G with RNAi experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Downregulation of Met in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation.
source: Downregulation of either gce or Met in adult progenitors abrogates post-mating proliferation (G, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G with RNAi experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Downregulation of gce in adult progenitors abrogates gut size increase.
source: and gut size increase (J, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, t-test with Holm's correction).

claim: Downregulation of Met in adult progenitors abrogates gut size increase.
source: and gut size increase (J, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi mated, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Met RNAi mated, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3J with RNAi experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is abolished by the downregulation of gce in ECs.
source: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is abolished by the downregulation of gce, but not Met, in ECs using the EC-specific driver Mex-Gal4 (K–K′′′′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3K with RNAi experiments in ECs.

claim: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is not abolished by the downregulation of Met in ECs.
source: The upregulation of bgm reporter upon mating is abolished by the downregulation of gce, but not Met, in ECs using the EC-specific driver Mex-Gal4 (K–K′′′′).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3K with RNAi experiments in ECs.

claim: JHa application in virgin females results in a net growth of the gut.
source: JHa application in virgin females results in a net growth of the gut, as shown by the increase in caudal-marked cells (A, p = 0.004, t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A with cell count data and statistical analysis.

claim: Using esgReDDM to specifically knockdown gce in adult intestinal progenitor cells abolishes the proliferative effect of JHa application.
source: Consequently, using esgReDDM to specifically knockdown gce in adult intestinal progenitor cells abolishes the proliferative effect of JHa application (C, C′)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,C' with RNAi experiments.

claim: Downregulation of gce does not reduce the number of progenitors after 7 days.
source: but does not reduce the number of progenitors after 7 days of downregulation (D, p > 0.05, t test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D with cell count data and statistical analysis.

claim: Progenitors in which gce is downregulated can still proliferate normally to replenish a gut damaged by paraquat.
source: Progenitors in which gce is downregulated can still proliferate normally to replenish a gut damaged by a 24 hr application of the toxin paraquat (E, E′ with quantification of mitoses in F, p < 0.001 for both esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > gce RNAi, p > 0.05 for all other relevant comparisons, t test with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,E',F with paraquat damage experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: The number of progenitors is not reduced by paraquat treatment.
source: and the number of progenitors is not reduced by this treatment (G, p = 0.04 between esgReDDM/+ untreated control and esgReDDM > gce RNAi untreated control, p > 0.05 for all other relevant comparisons, t test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G with cell count data and statistical analysis.

claim: The transcription factor Kruppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1) is transcriptionally upregulated after 3 days of mating.
source: The transcription factor Kruppel homolog 1 (Kr-h1), a well-established effector of JH responses, is transcriptionally upregulated after 3 days of mating (H, p = 0.02 in w1118, p = 0.02 in OregonR, paired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H with qPCR data and statistical analysis.

claim: Kr-h1 function is necessary for the re-sizing of the gut after mating.
source: Kr-h1 function is necessary and sufficient for the re-sizing of the gut after mating, as its downregulation in intestinal progenitors through RNA interference using esgReDDM prevents the increase in proliferation (I, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Kr-h1 RNAi mated, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction) and gut size (J, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Kr-h1 RNAi mated, t-test with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J with RNAi experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Kr-h1 function is sufficient for the re-sizing of the gut after mating.
source: while overexpression of Kr-h1 constructs from the same cells recapitulates the effect of mating in virgins (proliferation, I, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Kr-h1GS virgin, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Kr-h1UAS virgin, negative binomial GLM with Holm's correction; gut size J, p < 0.001 between esgReDDM/+ and esgReDDM > Kr-h1UAS virgin, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J with overexpression experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Downregulating gce constitutively from ECs significantly suppresses the transcriptional increase of the lipid metabolism gene bgm upon mating.
source: Downregulating gce constitutively from ECs using Mex-Gal4 significantly suppresses the transcriptional increase of the lipid metabolism gene bgm upon mating, as indicated by the intensity ranking of a gce reporter (L, p = 0.004 between gce RNAi/+ and Mex > gce RNAi, p = 0.02 between Mex > gce RNAi and Mex/KK control, Mann–Whitney test with Holm's correction; relevant comparisons with Met RNAi are not significant).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L with reporter data and statistical analysis.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,C,C' with experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Sterile females carrying the ovoD1 mutation experience the post-mating gut size increase.

claim: Sterile females carrying the ovoD1 mutation experience the post-mating SREBP reporter activation.

claim: Adult-specific downregulation of gce in ECs reduces the total progeny produced by females in the 6 days following their first mating.
source: The role of intestinal remodelling in enhancing reproductive capacity is confirmed with additional RNA interference lines against the JH receptor gce (chosen because of its larger effect in Figure 4E; F, p = 0.002 between GD11178/+ and Mexts> GD11178, p = 0.008 between Mexts > GD11178 and Mexts/+, p < 0.001 between GD47465/+ and Mexts> GD47465, p = 0.003 between Mexts > GD11178 and Mexts/+, t-test with Holm's correction)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F with fecundity data and statistical analysis.

claim: Adult-specific downregulation of SREBP in ECs reduces the total progeny produced by females in the 6 days following their first mating.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G with fecundity data and statistical analysis.

claim: Eggs laid by gce, Met, or SREBP RNAi mothers are viable.
source: Despite these effect on fecundity, eggs laid by gce, Met, or SREBP RNAi mothers are viable (H and I, mean hatched fraction >0.9 for all groups, p > 0.05 for all relevant comparisons, t-test).

claim: The amount of stored triglycerides (TAG) in the carcass of 3-day mated sterile female flies is increased compared to virgins.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,C with TLC data and statistical analysis.

claim: Adult-specific downregulation of Met in ECs reduces the total progeny produced by females in the 6 days following their first mating.
source: Adult-specific downregulation of JH receptors gce and Met or SREBP in ECs reduces the total progeny produced by females in the 6 days following their first mating (E, p = 0.01 between Met RNAi/+ and Mexts > Met RNAi, p = 0.007 between Mexts > Met RNAi and Mexts/KK control, p < 0.001 between gce RNAi/+ and Mexts > gce RNAi, p = 0.007 between Mexts> gce RNAi and Mexts/KK control
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with fecundity data and statistical analysis.

claim: Adult-specific downregulation of SREBP in ECs reduces the total progeny produced by females in the 6 days following their first mating.
source: F p = 0.04 between SREBP RNAi/+ and Mexts > SREBP RNAi, p = 0.04 between Mexts > SREBP RNAi and Mexts/TRiP control, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F with fecundity data and statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of the ovarian lipid sink in sterile ovoD1 virgin flies, treatment with JHa increases neutral lipid content in the posterior midgut.
source: In the absence of the ovarian lipid sink in sterile ovoD1 virgin flies, treatment with JHa increases neutral lipid content, as revealed by Oil Red O staining, in the posterior midgut (G, G′, quantified in H: p = 0.002, t-test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G,G',H with Oil Red O staining data and statistical analysis.

claim: Acute block of lipid export in virgin females results in heavy accumulation of neutral lipid in the posterior midgut region.
source: Acute block of lipid export by heat-shock activation of lpp > stop > LTP RNAi (Palm et al., 2012) in virgin females results in heavy accumulation of neutral lipid in this gut region, further indicating that this midgut region provides a net source of lipid in adult flies (I, quantified in J: p < 0.001 between LTP RNAi/+ and lpp > stop > LTP RNAi, p < 0.001 between lpp > stop > LTP RNAi and lpp > stop>/+, p < 0.001 between lpp > stop > LTP RNAi and lpp > stop > LTP RNAi heat shock control, t-test with Holm's correction).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I,J with Oil Red O staining data, statistical analysis, and a citation to previous work on the genetic manipulation.

claim: The posterior midgut region provides a net source of lipid in adult flies.
source: further indicating that this midgut region provides a net source of lipid in adult flies
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking lipid export leads to lipid accumulation in the posterior midgut.
